newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Christiana net profit falls 23 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Christiana net profit falls 23 pct.

text.p: Norway's second biggest commercial bank, Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse said on Wednesday restructuring costs and lower loan-loss write-backs cut its 1996 net profits by nearly 23 percent.
But net interest income, the bank's core business, rose despite narrowing interest margins in overbanked Norway.
Net profits fell to 2.15 billion crowns ($318.4 million) from 2.78 billion, corresponding to earnings per share of 3.91 crowns, down from 5.04 crowns in 1995.

"I am most satisfied with the bank's income side," chief executive officer Borger Lenth said in a statement. "We have succeeded in increasing the net interest income despite the keen competition in the market. In addition we see that non-interest income...shows a rising trend."
The board proposed raising the dividend to 1.55 crowns from 1.10 in 1995.
Christiania shares traded about two percent higher at 26.50 crowns in the early afternoon on the Oslo Bourse.
"The share price is up because of the higher dividend," an Oslo-based analyst said. "The result was moderately good."

Net interest income increased to 3.43 billion crowns from 3.30 billion while non-interest income, including commissions and fees, rose to 1.49 billion from 1.32 billion. Non-interest expenses, however, fell to 3.37 million crowns from 2.94 billion, mainly because of a restructuring charge of 228 million crowns.
"The charge of 228 million crowns...will be applied in making the bank more cost-efficient in the course of the next couple of years," Lenth said.
Profits were also burdened by a sharp reduction in the recovery of loans written off during a financial crisis that hit major Norwegian banks around 1990.
Write-backs, which have helped to sweeten the balance sheets of Christiania and other major Norwegian banks in the past few years, shrank to 575 million crowns from 1.09 billion in 1995.
Top banks were bailed out of the crisis by the government, which still keeps a controlling stake in Christiania and Den norske Bank (DnB) ) as a result of the rescue action.
Analyst expect the write-backs to run down as old non-performing loans vanish. Norwegian banks returned to profit two years ago amid an upturn in the national economy.
"Because of the write-backs and tax losses carried forward, Christiania has profits above normal levels today," one analyst said. "Normally the bank should have an EPS of 2.50 crowns."

Total non-performing commitments were reduced by 0.8 billion crowns to 2.9 billion in 1996. Losses on loans and guarantees where no specific loss allowance has been made amounted to 178 million crowns, down from 268 million in 1995.
